The key is *goal congruence* — "aligning of goals between a corporation's strategy and a manager's personal goals" (Ch 12.1). Performance measures should be based on *controllable factors* over which the manager has authority; evaluating managers on *uncontrollable factors* "will be demotivating and does not promote goal congruence" (Ch 12.1).

Characteristics of a good performance measurement system: based on activities the manager controls or influences; measurable; timely; consistently applied; comparable to budgeted results, standards, or past performance; not biased toward the manager over the company (Ch 12.2, "Identify the Characteristics of an Effective Performance Measure").

A Link to Learning feature reports that General Electric is changing its performance measurement practices to align more closely with the goals of millennials, pointing to an Impraise blog post on GE performance reviews [AE] (Ch 12.2, "Link to Learning").

The text catalogues limitations of traditional accounting-based measurement: results can be affected by manager actions (LIFO inventory timing example), by economic conditions outside manager control (currency-exchange effects), by multi-period decisions (capital budgeting), and by manager short-term focus when bonuses are tied to current-period results. The recommended remedy: combine accounting-based measures with non-accounting measures, short-term with long-term indicators, quantitative with qualitative components (Ch 12.1, "Potential Limitations of Traditional Performance Measurement").

### ROI, RI, EVA — fuller development

The *DuPont Model* decomposes ROI into two components: sales margin × asset turnover. *Sales margin* = net income / sales (how much profit per sales dollar). *Asset turnover* = sales / average operating assets (how many sales dollars per asset dollar). When multiplied, sales components cancel and the result is income / average operating assets, the standard ROI formula. The DuPont decomposition reveals different paths to high ROI: a jewellery store's high margin / low turnover versus a grocery store's low margin / high turnover (Ch 12.3, "Calculation and Interpretation of the Return on Investment").

ROI's drawback is the goal-congruence problem identified in Ch 9: a high-ROI segment may reject a project below its current ROI even when the project benefits the company. Residual income, computed as income - (invested capital × minimum required rate of return), addresses this by rewarding any positive contribution above the firm-wide threshold (Ch 12.3, "Calculation and Interpretation of the Residual Income").

*Economic value added (EVA)* is "similar to RI but is a measure of shareholder wealth that is being created by a project, segment, or division" (Ch 12.3, "Calculation and Interpretation of Economic Value Added"). EVA = after-tax income - (invested capital × weighted average cost of capital). The *weighted average cost of capital (WACC)* is "the cost that the company expects to pay on average to finance assets and growth using either debt or equity", weighted by the proportion of debt and equity in the capital structure. The text develops a worked example: with 45 per cent debt at 8 per cent and 55 per cent equity at 9.8 per cent, WACC = 9 per cent. EVA differs from RI in two ways: WACC reflects actual financing cost rather than a chosen minimum return; EVA uses after-tax income while RI typically uses pre-tax income (Ch 12.3).

The text discusses methodological complications: invested capital may be defined as fixed assets, productive assets (fixed plus inventory), or operating assets (productive plus intangibles plus current); valuation may be net book value, gross book value, or fair (market) value. Income may be operating income, EBIT, EBITDA, net income, or return on funds employed (ROFE). Each definition produces different numbers; the volume recommends consistency and alignment with manager controllability (Ch 12.3, "Considerations in Using the Three Evaluative Tools").

### The balanced scorecard

The balanced scorecard (BSC) was first proposed by Art Schneiderman of Analog Devices in 1987 and developed into its current form by Robert Kaplan and David Norton (Harvard) [BT] (Ch 12.4, "History and Function of the Balanced Scorecard"). Its claim: financial measures alone evaluate the past and can be gamed; *quantitative factors* (financial measures) plus *qualitative factors* (non-financial measures) across four perspectives produce more durable evaluation (Ch 12.4, "Four Components of a Balanced Scorecard").

The four perspectives:

1. **Financial perspective**: ROI, RI, EVA, EPS, revenue growth, sales growth, inventory turnover, or domain-specific measures (e.g., seat revenue for an airline).
2. **Internal business perspective**: defects, machine downtime, transaction efficiency, products completed per employee per day, or domain-specific measures (e.g., percentage of time planes are on the ground).
3. **Customer perspective**: customer satisfaction, repeat customers, new customers, customer referrals, market share.
4. **Learning and growth**: employee suggestions adopted, turnover rate, training hours, scope of process improvements, new products.

The BSC enables a *stakeholder perspective* rather than a stockholder-only perspective, with stakeholders defined as "people who are affected by the decisions made by a company, such as investors, creditors, managers, regulators, employees, customers, suppliers, and even laypeople who are concerned about whether or not the company is a good world citizen" (Ch 12.4, "Four Components of a Balanced Scorecard").

The volume's worked example (Scrumptious Sweets bakery) demonstrates BSC at three levels: corporate, divisional (brownie division), and individual (storefront employees) — each preserving the same four categories but increasing in goal specificity (Ch 12.4, "Combining the Four Components of a Balanced Scorecard"; Figures 12.6-12.8). The text emphasises that BSC design works best collaboratively, with employee input on goals and metrics, "rather than being told what goals are to be met" (Ch 12.4, "Combining the Four Components of a Balanced Scorecard").

> "The combination of these different types of quantitative and qualitative measures—project-specific measures, employee-level measures, divisional measures, and corporate measures—enables an organization to more adequately assess how it is progressing toward meeting short- and long-term goals."
> [V] (Ch 12.4, "Final Summary of Quantitative and Quantitative Performance Measurement Tools")

## Part XIII: Sustainability reporting (Ch 13)

### Sustainability and CSR

*Sustainability* is defined here as "meeting the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs" [V] (Ch 13.1, "Describe Sustainability and the Way It Creates Business Value", citing the Brundtland Commission Report 1987). *Corporate social responsibility* (CSR) is "the set of actions that firms take to assume responsibility for their impact on the environment and social well-being" (Ch 13.1).

The Paris Climate Agreement of December 2015 — "a historic plan to work together to limit the increase of global temperatures to 1.5 °C" adopted by 196 nations — anchors the contemporary international framing (Ch 13.1, "Describe Sustainability and the Way It Creates Business Value"). The text notes the United States's 2017 announced withdrawal and a coalition of 20 U.S. states and 50 cities (led by California governor Jerry Brown and former NYC mayor Michael Bloomberg) that pledged to continue supporting the Agreement (Ch 13.1).

Social media has widened what the public sees: "as a consequence of social media platforms such as Facebook and Twitter, the public is more aware of corporate behavior, both good and bad. Investors and consumers alike can make financial decisions about firms that align with their own values and beliefs" [V] (Ch 13.1, "Describe Sustainability and the Way It Creates Business Value").

Companies adopting sustainable practices may benefit through saving money on water and energy, lowering insurance costs, attracting investors, reducing social risks, improving customer loyalty, reducing regulation risk through proactive measures, attracting and retaining employees with shared values, strengthening community relationships, and improving environmental sustainability (Ch 13.1, "Sustainability Reporting").

### Three foundational corporate cases

The text develops three cases as historical drivers of contemporary sustainability reporting:

- **Union Carbide / Bhopal (1984)**: methyl isocyanate leak at the Bhopal pesticide plant exposed more than 600,000 people, with an official toll of 3,598 dead and 42,000 injured (some accounts: 16,000-20,000 deaths). The case "highlighted the power disparity between corporations and poor individuals and became a stark emblem of corporate disregard for the human toll of the quest for profit" (Ch 13.1, "Historical Drivers of Contemporary Sustainability Reporting"). Within days of the leak, CEO Warren Anderson "arrived in India, was arrested and released, and then immediately flew out of the country"; although charged with manslaughter, "he never returned to India to face trial" [V] (Ch 13.1, "Union Carbide"). Union Carbide ultimately paid $470 million in compensation; was bought by Dow Chemical in 2001. "More than thirty years later, many victims are still awaiting the compensation they were promised" [V] (Ch 13.1, "Union Carbide").
- **Nestlé / baby formula**: "Nestlé is the target of one of the longest-running consumer boycotts in modern history" [V] (Ch 13.1, "Nestlé"), originating in the mid-1970s when aggressive marketing of formula in developing countries led to mothers using contaminated water for preparation and having their breast milk dry up. UNICEF estimated formula-fed infants were "14 times more likely [...] to die of diarrhea and four times more likely to die of pneumonia than breast-fed children" [V] (Ch 13.1, "Nestlé"). The boycott prompted Nestlé to support WHO breastfeeding guidelines and adopt stricter internal policies.
- **Johnson & Johnson / Tylenol (1982)**: cyanide-laced Tylenol capsules killed seven people. CEO James Burke formed a strategy team asking "How do we protect the people?" and "How do we save the product?". The company first warned consumers through a national announcement not to take any Tylenol product, withdrew all Tylenol capsules in Chicago, and on finding two more compromised bottles ordered a nationwide withdrawal of all Tylenol products: "Less than a week had passed" [V]. At the same time it "established a toll-free number for consumers and another one for news organizations that provided daily recorded updates about the crisis" [V] (Ch 13.1, "Johnson & Johnson"). Within two months, Tylenol was relaunched with three-way tamper-proof packaging (Ch 13.1, "Johnson & Johnson"). The recall cost more than $100 million but the share price returned to its previous high within six weeks; the response is "lauded in business case studies and has formed the basis of crisis communications strategies developed by researchers" (Ch 13.1).

### The triple bottom line and information users

The *triple bottom line* (TBL or 3BL) was "first proposed in 1997 by John Elkington to expand the traditional financial reporting framework so as to capture a firm's social and environmental performance" [V] (Ch 13.1, "Initial Sustainability Reports"). Elkington's "People, Planet, Profit" formulation accompanies the framing. *Life-cycle* or *full-cost accounting* takes a "cradle to grave" approach including disposal costs and externalities.

Current reporting topics include the environment, human rights, employee relations, and philanthropy. On philanthropy, "many companies offer matching programs wherein they will match charitable contributions made by employees. Some companies also offer from two to five paid work days per year for employees to perform volunteer work" [V] (Ch 13.1, "Current Examples of Sustainability in Business"). Among the companies profiled as creating business value, Patagonia has for more than 30 years given 1 per cent of annual sales or 10 per cent of pre-tax profits, whichever is greater, to environmental organisations, and "In 2012, Patagonia became one of California's first B corporations" [V] (Ch 13.1, "Patagonia").

A Your Turn exercise, "Mars Inc.", has students review the company’s Sustainable in a Generation Plan and weigh the cost outlays of its sustainability measures against present or future savings. The sample solution lists three categories: Healthy Planet (climate action, water stewardship, land use, waste reduction), Thriving People (increasing income, respecting human rights, increasing opportunities for women) and Nourishing Wellbeing (product improvement, responsible marketing, food safety and security) [AE]. It notes that these measures may need significant short-term spending, cites Mars’s target to cut GHG emissions 67% by 2050 from 2015 levels, and says better raw-material production practices should raise efficiency and eventually lower costs [AE] (Ch 13.1, "Mars Inc.").

A Think It Through feature, "Do Friedman’s Ideas Stand the Test of Time?", quotes economist Milton Friedman’s 1970 New York Times Magazine argument that, for a manager acting as the business owner’s agent, "there is one and only one social responsibility of business—to use its resources and engage in activities designed to increase its profits so long as it stays within the rules of the game, which is to say, engages in open and free competition without deception or fraud" [V] [BT, Friedman]. It asks students whether, given what has since been learned about Earth’s environment, the view that the "sole purpose of business is to make profits" [V] still holds (Ch 13.1, "Do Friedman’s Ideas Stand the Test of Time?").

The triple bottom line "expanded the role of reporting beyond shareholders and investors to a broader range of stakeholders – that is, anyone directly or indirectly affected by the organization, including employees, customers, government entities, regulators, creditors, and the local community" [V] (Ch 13.2, "Identify User Needs for Information"). Primary information users are shareholders and lenders; secondary users are customers, suppliers, governments and regulators, the community, and employees.

User-by-user analysis (Ch 13.2):

- **Shareholders**: focus on future viability and value retention; use ratios like P/E, EPS, ROI; ethical-investment movement is growing — "in 2016, ethical investments topped $8.7 trillion, up 33% from 2014, and they now account for 20% of all investment under professional management" [V] (Ch 13.2, "Shareholders"). The Forum for Sustainable and Responsible Investment defines sustainable investing as one that "considers environmental, social and corporate governance criteria to generate long-term competitive financial returns and positive societal impact" (Ch 13.2, "Ethical Considerations: Millennials Are Demanding Sustainable Investments"). "A recent Harvard Business Review study showed that socially responsible companies post higher profits and stock performance than those that were not focused on social responsibility" [V], a result the text says is supported by a Deutsche Bank analysis of more than 2,000 studies dating to the 1970s, "90% of which suggested that socially responsible investing gives better returns than passive investing" [V] (Ch 13.2).
- **Lenders**: want to know going-concern risk; geographic concentration risk; human-rights-violation exposure.
- **Employees**: increasingly want to work for value-aligned companies. "In 2016, 76% of millennials said that a company's social and environmental commitments were considerations in employment, with 64% of millennials indicating that they would not work for a company that did not have strong corporate social responsibility practices" [V] (Ch 13.2, "Employees").
- **Customers**: want value-aligned products. A 2016 Unilever study showed "33% of consumers buy from brands they believe are doing social or environmental good and that this presents a €966 billion (over 1.1 trillion $USD) opportunity for brands" [V] (Ch 13.2, "Customers").
- **Governments and regulators**: want to see responsible behaviour to reduce the need for restrictive legislation. "Many companies form industry alliance groups that aim to implement best practices in trade, social responsibility, or environmental initiatives" [V] (Ch 13.2, "Governments and Regulators").
- **Community**: reflects the *social contract* — "the expectation that companies will hold to an unwritten contract with society as a whole" [V]; "If a firm is undertaking actions that might harm society or that reject its general values, community backlash may cost the firm dearly" [V] (Ch 13.2, "Community").

The text concludes Ch 13.2 with the framing claim: "a company's accountability to a wider group of users is an element of stakeholder theory. This theory presents a view that asserts a corporation has an obligation to groups beyond just its shareholders" [V] (Ch 13.2, "Community"). The *public benefit corporation* model emerges as an alternative legal structure that "broadens the perspective of traditional corporate law by incorporating concepts of purpose, accountability and transparency with respect to all corporate stakeholders, not just stockholders" [V] (Ch 13.2, "Ethical Considerations: Public Benefit Corporations").

### Three reporting frameworks

Three sustainability reporting frameworks are catalogued:

- **Global Reporting Initiative (GRI)** (formed 1997). According to GRI, "92% of the Global 250 produced sustainability reports in 2016" (Ch 13.3, "Global Reporting Initiative (GRI)"). GRI's 2016 standards include three universal standards (foundation, general disclosures, management approach) plus topic-specific standards selected based on materiality. GRI defines materiality as: "The report should cover Aspects that: Reflect the organization's significant economic, environmental and social impacts; or substantively influence the assessments and decisions of stakeholders" [V] (Ch 13.3, citing GRI).
- **Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB)** (established 2011). Targeted at investor-focused reporting; available for 79 industries across 10 sectors. SASB adopted the U.S. Supreme Court's view of materiality (TSC Indus. v. Northway): "a substantial likelihood that the disclosure of the omitted fact would have been viewed by the reasonable investor as having significantly altered the 'total mix' of information made available" [V] (Ch 13.3, "Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB)").
- **Integrated Reporting** (International Integrated Reporting Council, formed 2010). Brings together "financial, social, environmental and governance information in a clear, concise, consistent and comparable format" (Ch 13.3, "Integrated Reporting"). The framework identifies six categories of capital: financial, manufactured, intellectual, human, social and relationship, natural. Materiality starts with "Identifying relevant matters based on their ability to affect value creation" [V], then evaluates their importance, prioritises them, and decides what to disclose (Ch 13.3, "Integrated Reporting"). Mandatory in South Africa and Brazil; adopted by Clorox, Entergy, GE, Jones Lang LaSalle, PepsiCo, Prudential Financial, Southwest Airlines.

### Future issues

Sustainability reporting "is still relatively new and its use is not yet mandatory" but is converging on materiality-based disclosure. The text projects future issues in cybersecurity (the need for "security against cyberattacks, which not only harm the company's functioning but also dent consumer confidence" [V]), globalisation under shifting political winds, and artificial intelligence's impact on white-collar work, which "will raise a number of ethical questions, such as whether corporations have a greater responsibility to society than to shareholders" [V] — citing Bill Gates's call for a robot tax to finance a Universal Basic Income, and Yanis Varoufakis's concept of a Universal Basic Dividend funded by a portion of corporate IPOs (Ch 13.4, "Future Issues in Sustainability"). The chapter closes with the framing that "[s]ocial responsibility reporting has moved us a long way from merely reporting the financial results of businesses"; it provides a foundation linking all businesses to all citizens, and "it helps bind us all in a way that says we are all truly part of a single, global environment that is determined by the actions of both businesses and citizens" [V] (Ch 13.4).

> "In short, sustainability reporting has evolved to describe both how the company's practices contribute to the social good and how they add value to the company, which ultimately provides better returns to its investors."
> [V] (Ch 13.1, "Sustainability Reporting")

## Appendix A: Financial statement analysis

Financial statement analysis "reviews financial information found on financial statements to make informed decisions about the business" (App A, "Financial Statement Analysis"). Three primary tools: horizontal analysis (trend analysis across periods), vertical analysis (line-item proportions within a period), and financial ratios.

### Horizontal and vertical analysis

*Horizontal analysis* compares one period (typically the prior year as base) to a current year via dollar change and percentage change. Multiple periods are needed to identify a trend (App A, "Horizontal Analysis"). *Vertical analysis* expresses each line item as a percentage of a base — net sales for income statements, total assets and total liabilities-plus-equity for balance sheets — producing common-size statements that facilitate cross-company comparison (App A, "Vertical Analysis").

### Four ratio categories

Ratios fall into four categories (App A, "Overview of Financial Ratios"):

- **Liquidity ratios**: working capital (current assets - current liabilities), current ratio (current assets / current liabilities), quick ratio (current assets less inventory and prepaid / current liabilities). Show ability to pay short-term obligations.
- **Solvency ratios**: debt-to-equity (total liabilities / total equity), times interest earned (EBIT / interest expense). Show ability to meet long-term obligations.
- **Efficiency ratios**: accounts receivable turnover (net credit sales / average accounts receivable), total asset turnover (net sales / average total assets), inventory turnover (cost of goods sold / average inventory), days' sales in inventory (365 / inventory turnover). Show how well assets are managed.
- **Profitability ratios**: profit margin (net income / net sales), return on total assets (net income / average total assets), return on equity (net income - preferred dividends / average stockholders' equity). Show returns on operations.

### Limits of the analysis

The text cautions that "past performance does not always dictate future performance"; that economic influences (inflation, recession) can skew numbers; and that companies' reporting practices may shift over time, sometimes invisibly within published statements (App A, "Advantages and Disadvantages of Financial Statement Analysis").

## Connections the author makes in the text

- **Eliyahu Goldratt's Theory of Constraints** — cited approvingly as a "valuable instrument for improving the flaws in processes" with five focusing steps for continuous improvement [BT] (Ch 1.5, "Lean Practices").
- **Toyota Motor Corporation** — origin of just-in-time manufacturing and lean practices; "implemented by the Japanese automaker, Toyota Motor Corporation, soon after the end of World War II" [BT] (Ch 1.5).
- **Motorola** — origin of Six Sigma in 1986 and continued LSS training centre [BT] (Ch 1.5).
- **John Elkington** — triple bottom line; "first proposed in 1997 by John Elkington to expand the traditional financial reporting framework" [BT] (Ch 13.1).
- **Brundtland Commission Report (1987)** — sustainable development definition; "the resulting Brundtland Commission Report laid the groundwork for the concept of sustainable development" [BT] (Ch 13.1).
- **Robert Kaplan and David Norton** — current four-perspective balanced scorecard development at Harvard [BT] (Ch 12.4).
- **Art Schneiderman / Analog Devices** — earlier balanced scorecard origin in 1987 with three categories [BT] (Ch 12.4).
- **Chris Argyris** — double-loop learning concept introduced in 1977 HBR article, framed as a comprehensive evaluation that asks whether current goals should be adjusted [BT] (Ch 9.1).
- **Yvon Chouinard / Patagonia / Tin Shed Ventures** — B-corp pioneer; "for more than 30 years, [...] Patagonia has donated 1% of its annual sales or 10% of its pre-tax profits, whichever is greater" [BT] (Ch 13.1).
- **U.S. Supreme Court (TSC Indus. v. Northway, 1976)** — materiality definition adopted by SASB [BT] (Ch 13.3).
- **WHO International Code of Marketing of Breast-Milk Substitutes** — Nestlé's stricter internal policy basis [BT] (Ch 13.1).
- **GRI / SASB / IIRC** — three sustainability reporting frameworks each with distinct materiality definitions [BT] (Ch 13.3).
- **Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum)** — technological revolution framing [BT] (Ch 13.4).
- **Bill Gates** — robot tax proposal to fund UBI [BT] (Ch 13.4).
- **Yanis Varoufakis** — Universal Basic Dividend concept [BT] (Ch 13.4).
- **Walker and Fleischman (2013)** — ethics in budgeting research; "the existence of formal ethical codes, ethics training, good management role models, and social pressure to be disclosing within an organization can be a deterrent to budget manipulation" [BT] (Ch 7.5, citing Walker et al., Management Accounting Quarterly).
- **Cohen and Pant (2018)** — long-term variance analysis perspective [BT] (Ch 8.5).
- **Hitt and Collins (2007)** — pro-stakeholder culture and ethical decision-making [BT] (Ch 9.4, citing Business Horizons).

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *Pure absorption costing for managerial decisions.* The text frames absorption costing as required by GAAP but inferior for internal decision-making because it can mask the impact of fixed costs and create incentives to overproduce: "the Big Three auto companies made decisions based on absorption costing, and the result was the manufacturing of more vehicles than the market demanded" (Ch 6.5, "Absorbing Costs through Overproduction").
- *Equal allocation of common costs in segment evaluation.* The SnowBucks worked example is the volume's central illustration that equal common-cost allocation can produce false signals about segment unprofitability; relevant-cost and contribution-margin analysis reveal the misleading allocation (Ch 10.4).
- *Sole reliance on ROI as a segment evaluation measure.* The text argues that ROI alone produces goal-incongruence problems: a high-ROI segment manager will reject a project that benefits the company because it lowers the segment's average ROI. Residual income and EVA are positioned as remedies (Ch 9.3, Ch 12.3).
- *Pure financial-measure performance evaluation.* The balanced scorecard's case rests on the claim that financial measures alone are gameable, lagging, and short-term-biased; non-financial measures across four perspectives produce more durable evaluation (Ch 12.1, "Potential Limitations of Traditional Performance Measurement"; Ch 12.4).
- *Stockholder-only accountability.* Sustainability reporting is framed as a corrective to financial-only reporting that ignores wider stakeholder interests; the public benefit corporation model is presented as a legal expression of the same correction (Ch 13.1, Ch 13.2).
- *Pure cost-minimisation in ethical decisions.* The Ford Pinto case is the volume's central illustration that "more than cost and revenue should be considered when making an ethical business decision"; quantitative cost-benefit analysis that excludes ethical and reputational consequences produces decisions that look profitable in the short term and disastrous in the long term (Ch 10.6, "Ethical Considerations: When to Include a Lifesaving Option").
- *Budget slack and managing-to-the-variance.* The text repeatedly warns that variance-based evaluation can be gamed via inflated standards (slack) or via short-term decisions that meet variance targets at the cost of long-term goals (Ch 7.5, Ch 8.5).
- *Ideal standards as motivators.* Ideal standards "may see this level as unattainable" and are not the best motivator; attainable standards are recommended (Ch 8.1, "Fundamentals of Standard Costs").

## Citation and source-integrity notes

This deep reference was produced via a 9-pass ingestion protocol against a pymupdf4llm 0.2.9 conversion of the OpenStax PDF, which dropped framed feature boxes; the source has since been re-converted (2026-10-16, PyMuPDF text blocks; see the source card). On 2026-10-17 the spans that re-conversion restored were listed by an order-aware word diff of the old and new conversions (runs of 8 or more inserted words), checked against the old text so moved text did not count, and sorted by section; the spans in this reference's coverage were read in full, as the Coverage line records. Citation style is `(Ch N, "Section name")` because that conversion did not preserve PDF page anchors.

Coverage is partial in the sense that pedagogical scaffolding (per-chapter Key Terms, Summary, Multiple Choice, Questions, Exercise Sets, Problem Sets, Thought Provokers, Answer Key, and the PV/FV table appendices and Suggested Resources appendix and Index back-matter) is excluded by Option B coverage policy. Substantive content (chapter introductions, all numbered substantive sections, in-chapter features, and Appendix A) is included in full. Where this deep reference cites an OpenStax-stated statistic or claim, the text is the immediate source; where the OpenStax text in turn cites an external source (KPMG, GRI, UNICEF, IMA, etc.), the citation is given as `[V] (Ch N, "Section", citing X)` to make the borrowed-through chain explicit.
